name: velk
author: crafts-agent (braids, knots, over/under crossings)
description: PRIVATE. velk v2 = a plait of 4-6 lettered strands, drawn the way a plait is drawn on paper: at every crossing BOTH strands lean in and only the front one's line carries on through the middle, so the strand that goes behind is visibly BROKEN. Clue 'LETTERS|n': the distinct capitals are the strands left-to-right at the top of the plait (4, 5 or 6 of them) and n is uniform in 2..5. The answer is the whole plait as text rows. Row 0 is the clue's letters spaced out ('K Q R M'). Then, repeating in blocks of three: a LEAN row (the two strands that are about to cross show '\' and '/' at their OWN columns; every strand standing still shows '|' at its own column), a CROSS row (one mark in the gap column between that pair -- '\' if the LEFT strand of the pair passes in front, '/' if the right one does; the other strand's line simply stops), and the new STRAND row (the row above with those two letters swapped). Trailing spaces, blank lines at either end and CRLF are tolerated; leading indentation is not. LAW 'TAKE TURNS': every strand alternates over and under across its OWN successive crossings -- a strand that passed in front the last time it crossed must go behind the next time it crosses, and vice versa. LAW 'NO UNPICKING': two crossings in a row may not be at the same gap. COUNT: exactly n crossings have the strand named by the clue's FIRST letter passing in front; crossings where that strand goes under and crossings it is not part of are decoys and appear in every demo. INTENDED DISCOVERY PATH: demo 1 gives the layout, the clue-row anchoring and the swap consistency, and (this is the v2 change) the broken under-strand makes over/under readable without decoding a lone slash. Then n is hunted -- 'number of crossings' dies on its first probe, 'crossings involving the first strand' dies soon after, and 'crossings where that strand is in front' survives. TAKE TURNS and NO UNPICKING never appear in a demo and can only be found by probing. WHY v2: in run lad-velk-v1-1 both Opus players cracked v1 (100% final; velk1a in round 2 on 2 demos, velk1b in round 5 on 5 demos). v1's law 1 was GLOBAL ('the strand in front at one crossing may not be in front at the next'), which let velk1a build the degenerate witness it wrote up as 'exactly 2k-1 crossings, strictly ALTERNATING: the clue strand crosses at 1,3,5,... and is always in front, any other pair fills the even slots' -- it never had to read the mark as over/under at all ('\ = hunt moves right, / = hunt moves left'). velk1b's witness was 'rotate the word right by 2 with the minimal adjacent swaps, then pad with n-2 repetitions of the swaps [0,2,0,2], every crossing drawn \', and it recorded 'the true underlying invariant was never pinned down'. Making law 1 PER STRAND kills both outright: the clue strand cannot be in front at every one of its own crossings once n >= 2, and no strand can be behind at every one of its own crossings either. Measured over 1500 fresh clues: velk1a's family 0.0%, velk1b's family 0.0%, v1's solve() output re-scored 0.0%, v1's exact rule 5.2%. Other hypotheses, each solving its own version of the puzzle: 'n = the clue strand in front of its RIGHT-hand neighbour' 65.3% (a narrower reading of the same quantity -- a player there has essentially the right idea); 'the clue strand alternates and crosses every single time' (zig-zag sweep) 31.7%, which needs the whole insight and still only fits clues with K-1 >= 2n-1 gaps; 'n = crossings the clue strand goes UNDER' 28.4% and mark semantics inverted 27.2% (taking turns makes a strand's fronts and unders differ by at most one, so these two are near-misses by construction); 'n = number of backslashes' 17.3%; 'n = crossings the LAST strand is in front' 14.1%; right count + take-turns but no gap law 8.3%; both laws but count ignored 5.7%; right count + gap law but no take-turns 2.8%; right count and neither law 1.0%; 'n = crossings the clue strand is IN' 0.0%; a plait of exactly n crossings 0.0%; best constant answer 0.25%; a demo answer replayed under another clue 0.0%; all junk, truncations and shuffles 0%. The exact rule with a one-pass greedy scores 100%. The 1-30% band is a real gradient to climb: each law found roughly triples the hit-rate, so a player is never blind. Degenerate witnesses closed: empty string, the clue, row 0 alone (n >= 2 needs crossings), any constant picture (row 0 must be the clue's letters), a replayed demo, 'n crossings with the clue strand in front every time' (TAKE TURNS forbids it), and 'alternate a counted crossing with a free filler' (the filler is no longer free -- its two strands must be taking turns as well). The kid-judge note on v1 (2.8/5: 'use a braid convention kids know, visibly broken under-strand, so who is on top reads without decoding \ vs /') is what the two-row crossing block is for; the difficulty now sits entirely in the two laws and in which crossings count. solve() plans the counted crossings as a random non-adjacent subset of a randomly sized plait (3n-2..3n+5 crossings) and then walks a random legal plait, so demos are long, varied and full of decoys, and never the minimal witness. Deterministic generator; property-based scorer (any plait obeying both laws with the right count scores 1); score 504/512 chars, worst score call 0.12 ms, solve 0.16 ms mean / 1.5 ms worst, answers 100-729 chars. 11500 (clue, answer) pairs agree with an independent re-implementation of the rule written from this prose. Author direction: crafts / hands-on physical intuition.
solve:
def solve(clue):
    r"""Plait the strands of the clue so the first one comes out in front n times.

    Row 0 is the clue's letters spaced out.  A crossing is drawn the way a plait is
    drawn on paper, in two rows: a LEAN row where the two strands about to cross tip
    towards each other (`\` at the left one's own column, `/` at the right one's), and
    a CROSS row carrying a single mark in the gap between them -- the line of the
    strand that passes IN FRONT, carrying on through the middle (`\` = the left one
    carries on, `/` = the right one does).  The strand that goes behind is simply
    BROKEN: its line stops at the crossing and picks up again as a letter in the
    strand row underneath, which is the row above with the two letters swapped.

    Two laws, neither of which a demo can ever contradict (demos are positive only):
      * TAKE TURNS: every strand alternates -- each time a strand crosses it must be
        on the opposite side (in front / behind) from its own previous crossing;
      * NO UNPICKING: two crossings in a row may not be at the same gap.

    COUNT: exactly n crossings have the strand named by the clue's first letter in
    front.  Taking turns is what makes this hard to fake: that strand cannot be in
    front at every one of its own crossings, so a scoring plait needs at least 2n-1
    crossings and the counted ones must be interleaved with crossings where the clue
    strand goes UNDER, plus crossings it is not part of at all.  And the filler is not
    free either: every other strand has to keep taking turns too.

    Construction: plan the counted positions first (a random non-adjacent subset of a
    randomly sized plait, via the standard gap bijection), drop one 'clue strand goes
    under' crossing between each consecutive pair (and sometimes one before the
    first), then walk the plait picking uniformly among the legal crossings that fit
    the plan; retry on a dead end.
    """
    f, ns = clue.split("|")
    n = int(ns)
    K = len(f)
    X = f[0]
    W = 2 * K - 1
    r = random.Random(clue)
    bar = "".join("|" if e % 2 == 0 else " " for e in range(W))
    for _ in range(500):
        L = 3 * n - 2 + r.randint(0, 7)
        cut = sorted(r.sample(range(L - 2 * n + 2), n))
        pos = [v + 2 * i for i, v in enumerate(cut)]
        want = {}
        for c0 in pos:
            want[c0] = 1
        for i in range(n - 1):
            want[r.randint(pos[i] + 1, pos[i + 1] - 1)] = -1
        if pos[0] and r.random() < 0.5:
            want[r.randint(0, pos[0] - 1)] = -1
        p = list(f)
        side = {}
        q = -2
        rows = [" ".join(p)]
        ok = True
        for i in range(L):
            w = want.get(i, 0)
            M = []
            for j in range(K - 1):
                if j == q:
                    continue
                a, b = p[j], p[j + 1]
                for d in (0, 1):
                    fr, bk = (a, b) if d == 0 else (b, a)
                    if side.get(fr) == 1 or side.get(bk) == 0:
                        continue
                    if (1 if fr == X else -1 if bk == X else 0) != w:
                        continue
                    M.append((j, d, fr, bk))
            if not M:
                ok = False
                break
            j, d, fr, bk = r.choice(M)
            g = 2 * j + 1
            rows.append((bar[:g - 1] + "\\ /" + bar[g + 2:]).rstrip())
            rows.append((bar[:g - 1] + " " + "\\/"[d] + " " + bar[g + 2:]).rstrip())
            p[j], p[j + 1] = p[j + 1], p[j]
            rows.append(" ".join(p))
            side[fr] = 1
            side[bk] = 0
            q = j
        if ok:
            return "\n".join(rows)
    return ""
